title: ‘The Child Is Terrified’: Measles Doctors Speak Out
gist: Confirmed US measles cases hit a 35-year high by July 2026 and the US no longer meets a core criterion for measles elimination, with Utah's outbreak running since June 2025; six Utah pediatricians describe hospitalized unvaccinated children, the collapse of trust driving hesitancy, and the ACIP shake-up and HHS schedule changes that made it worse. Clinicians say the fix is consistent, state-funded messaging and compassionate conversation, not exclusion or fact-dumping.

insights.claim: Confirmed US measles cases hit a 35-year high by July 2026, and cases across 2025-2026 combined exceed the total of the previous 25 years.
insights.speaker: Amy Maxmen, KFF Health News
insights.so_what: A two-decade public-health gain reversing in two years resets baseline demand for MMR vaccine, pediatric hospital capacity and outbreak-response spending.
insights.locator: This isn’t just a bad year for measles

insights.claim: For the first time in 25 years the US fails a main criterion for measles elimination, which requires sporadic outbreaks to fizzle within a year; Utah's outbreak has run since June 2025.
insights.speaker: Amy Maxmen, KFF Health News
insights.so_what: Loss of elimination status is a discrete, dateable event that changes international travel-health guidance and state vaccination policy pressure.
insights.quote: That status hinges on sporadic outbreaks fizzling out within a year
insights.locator: For the first time in a quarter century

insights.claim: Nearly 400 people have been hospitalized with measles in the US across this year and last, three have died, and at least three suffered brain swelling with lingering symptoms.
insights.speaker: Amy Maxmen, KFF Health News
insights.so_what: Hospitalization counts, not case counts, are what drive pediatric ICU load and the cost line that insurers and hospital systems absorb.
insights.locator: Nearly 400 people have been hospitalized

insights.claim: The CDC is finalizing a comprehensive measles study covering January 2025 through June 2026 that will be reviewed by a national committee of measles specialists and then sent to the Pan American Health Organization.
insights.speaker: Amy Maxmen, KFF Health News
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete near-term catalyst calendar for the formal elimination-status decision.
insights.locator: This month, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is set to finalize

insights.claim: A CDC scientist with knowledge of the agency's internal measles report says continuous transmission over the past 12 months cannot credibly be denied.
insights.speaker: CDC scientist with knowledge of the agency’s measles report (unnamed by WIRED)
insights.so_what: An insider signalling the conclusion ahead of publication means the official downgrade is a formality, not a coin flip.
insights.quote: I don’t think we could say with a straight face that there hasn’t been transmission over the past 12 months
insights.locator: said a CDC scientist with knowledge of the agency’s measles report

insights.claim: Anne Schuchat, who led the CDC's immunization and respiratory disease group from 2006 to 2015, says the Pan American Health Organization's November assessment is a scheduling issue rather than an open question.
insights.speaker: Anne Schuchat
insights.so_what: Front-runs the headline: the loss of elimination status is effectively already decided before the fall meeting.
insights.quote: The assessment for elimination isn’t until November, but that is a scheduling issue, basically
insights.locator: The Pan American Health Organization will make its decisions at an annual meeting this fall

insights.claim: Hospital pediatricians say unvaccinated children presenting with fever or breathing trouble force far more aggressive workups — extra blood work and lumbar punctures to rule out meningitis — because their baseline risk of life-threatening illness is higher.
insights.speaker: Nathan Money, hospital pediatrician in Salt Lake County and Utah County
insights.so_what: Falling vaccination rates raise cost-per-encounter and invasive-procedure volume in pediatrics, not just case counts.
insights.locator: If the child has a fever or trouble breathing, and they’re unvaccinated

insights.claim: Measles presentation in hospitalized children includes 'tripoding' — the child hunched over, mouth open, drooling, dehydrated past producing tears, with labored breathing and retractions — a picture clinicians had largely stopped seeing.
insights.speaker: Emilie Morris, hospital pediatrician in Salt Lake County and Utah County
insights.so_what: Front-line description is the qualitative evidence public-health messaging campaigns will be built on.
insights.locator: On Unvaccinated Children Hospitalized With Measles Complications

insights.claim: A pediatric infectious disease specialist says even the best possible course of measles is one of the worst diseases most children ever go through, with the child unable to rest because the cough keeps them awake.
insights.speaker: Trahern W. Jones, pediatric infectious disease specialist in Salt Lake City
insights.so_what: Counters the 'measles is mild' narrative that underpins hesitancy — the core contested claim in vaccine demand.
insights.quote: Even the best possible course is going to be one of the worst diseases most children ever go through.
insights.locator: So I’m coming into a room and just hearing the most awful barking cough

insights.claim: One measles family was uninsured by choice because they did not expect to need the medical system, and cost was factoring into whether their child with pneumonia received oxygen.
insights.speaker: Emilie Morris, hospital pediatrician in Salt Lake County and Utah County
insights.so_what: Vaccine refusal correlates with insurance opt-out, concentrating uncompensated care on hospitals in outbreak counties.
insights.locator: One child was from a family that was uninsured

insights.claim: When exposure is caught too late for post-exposure vaccination, the fallback is a 21-day household quarantine of the remaining unvaccinated siblings — no grocery store, not even with a mask.
insights.speaker: Emilie Morris, hospital pediatrician in Salt Lake County and Utah County
insights.so_what: Quantifies the containment cost per household once a case is missed — the economic argument for prevention.
insights.locator: so then our recommendation was to quarantine their children at home for 21 days

insights.claim: Most non-vaccinating families are hesitant rather than aggressively anti-vax: younger, digital-native parents 'research' for months and get their concerns confirmed on social media.
insights.speaker: Tim Duffy, pediatrician in Salt Lake County
insights.so_what: The addressable population is persuadable, which is why messaging spend rather than mandates is the lever clinicians are asking for.
insights.quote: Younger parents who grew up in the digital age have done their research—“research” in quotation marks—for months.
insights.locator: A lot of families aren’t aggressively anti-vax, but they’re hesitant

insights.claim: A common path to under-vaccination is a pause after someone the family knows had what they believed was a vaccine reaction, with intent to catch up later that never happens.
insights.speaker: Trahern W. Jones, pediatric infectious disease specialist in Salt Lake City
insights.so_what: Identifies the intervention point — catch-up scheduling — that is cheaper than converting committed refusers.
insights.locator: The parents tell me they’re not anti-vaccine, but in the past

insights.claim: Parents' only prior knowledge of measles often comes from a grandmother who nursed children through it decades ago, showing institutional memory of the disease has been lost within two generations.
insights.speaker: Trahern W. Jones, pediatric infectious disease specialist in Salt Lake City
insights.so_what: Explains why risk perception collapsed even as vaccine efficacy stayed constant — memory decay, not new evidence.
insights.locator: In another case, the parent was stunned by how awful it was

insights.claim: Pediatricians attribute non-vaccination to lost trust in the medical community and trust placed elsewhere, with bad information coming from federal leadership as well as online sources.
insights.speaker: Nathan Money, hospital pediatrician in Salt Lake County and Utah County
insights.so_what: Names the federal government itself as a source of the misinformation — a policy risk that persists across administrations.
insights.quote: These are well-meaning parents who love their children, who have gotten bad information from federal leadership or from online sources.
insights.locator: It’s heartbreaking to see these children struggling to survive

insights.claim: The clinical rebuttal offered to autism-concerned parents is that if vaccines caused autism there would be more autism among vaccinated than unvaccinated children, and that is not observed.
insights.speaker: Pediatrician in southern Utah (unnamed by WIRED)
insights.so_what: The specific framing clinicians report as effective — useful for any campaign modeling persuasion.
insights.locator: A lot of parents are concerned about autism

insights.claim: In January the Department of Health and Human Services recommended reducing the number of vaccines given to children, and a federal judge blocked those changes a few months later.
insights.speaker: Amy Maxmen, KFF Health News
entities: Department of Health and Human Services
insights.so_what: A recommendation reversed by litigation leaves the schedule legally intact but publicly contested — the worst case for uptake.
insights.locator: [In January, the Department of Health and Human Services controversially recommended

insights.claim: The entire membership of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices was let go and a new panel selected, after which a couple of individuals changed vaccine recommendations outside the time-tested, evidence-based process.
insights.speaker: Pediatrician in southern Utah (unnamed by WIRED)
insights.so_what: Process capture at ACIP is the transmission channel from politics to actual pediatric vaccine demand.
insights.quote: A couple of individuals changed the recommendation outside of the time-tested, evidence-based process for evaluating vaccines.
insights.locator: I’ve said there was a process for the approval of immunizations through ACIP

insights.claim: The American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Academy of Family Physicians and several other professional organizations have issued statements that the schedule changes are not based on evidence.
insights.speaker: Pediatrician in southern Utah (unnamed by WIRED)
insights.so_what: A formal split between professional bodies and the federal schedule creates two competing standards of care for payers and clinicians.
insights.locator: I tell parents that the American Academy of Pediatrics

insights.claim: Vaccines have become a political football in a way that was not true 20 years ago, deliberately used to drive a wedge between groups.
insights.speaker: Trahern W. Jones, pediatric infectious disease specialist in Salt Lake City
insights.so_what: Politicization means vaccination rates now track partisan geography, making outbreak risk regionally concentrated and forecastable.
insights.quote: Vaccines have become a political football. That wasn’t true 20 years ago.
insights.locator: On the Influence of Politics on Vaccine Hesitancy

themes.theme: What clinicians say would reverse it

insights.claim: Pediatricians want state-sponsored MMR advertising on TV, billboards, schools, public buildings, grocery stores and at sports events, arguing state leadership on messaging has been 'pretty absent'.
insights.speaker: Nathan Money, hospital pediatrician in Salt Lake County and Utah County
insights.so_what: Points at a concrete, fundable gap — paid public-health media — that state budgets could fill and that would be visible in uptake data.
insights.quote: Right now, people have to go out of their way to find information from reputable sources.
insights.locator: We need consistent messaging from state leadership

insights.claim: Rebuilding vaccine trust requires consistent messaging at every level simultaneously — pediatricians, local health departments, community, city, district, religious and educational leadership.
insights.speaker: Nathan Money, hospital pediatrician in Salt Lake County and Utah County
insights.so_what: Sets the bar for what a credible recovery plan looks like; anything narrower predicts continued decline.
insights.locator: People are not vaccinated, because they’ve lost trust in the medical community

insights.claim: The persuasion technique clinicians report works is compassion and open-ended questions about the parent's experience, explicitly not citing facts, figures and guidelines.
insights.speaker: Trahern W. Jones, pediatric infectious disease specialist in Salt Lake City
insights.so_what: Evidence-dumping is counterproductive — relevant to how any institution should design vaccine communication.
insights.quote: I think it’s really important to not come down on them, citing facts and figures and pointing to guidelines on why they need to get their kids vaccinated.
insights.locator: Advice on Talking With Parents Who Don’t Vaccinate Their Children

insights.claim: Excluding unvaccinated children from a practice ends any future discussion and pushes those families toward like-minded doctors, making the overall situation worse.
insights.speaker: Ellie Brownstein, pediatrician in Salt Lake County and president-elect of the Utah chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics
insights.so_what: Argues against the exclusion policies many practices adopted — a live operational debate inside pediatric groups.
insights.quote: I don’t like the idea of excluding unvaccinated kids from my practice.
insights.locator: Brownstein: I don’t like the idea of excluding unvaccinated kids

insights.claim: A pediatric infectious disease specialist predicts more diseases previously considered eliminated will return, and that the dramatic changes needed to prevent that are not being made by those in power.
insights.speaker: Trahern W. Jones, pediatric infectious disease specialist in Salt Lake City
insights.so_what: Extends the trade beyond measles: pertussis, rubella and others become the next re-emergence candidates.
insights.quote: I think we’ll see more diseases start coming back that we thought we had gotten rid of.
insights.locator: On Being on the Frontier of Measles Returning to the US
